newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A - Part I -- CPI, enterprise zones.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A - Part I -- CPI, enterprise zones.

text.p: Following are excerpts from the question and answer session of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan before the House Banking Monetary Policy subcommittee on Wednesday.
Greenspan delivered the second and final leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins address at 1400 EST/1900 GMT.

GREENSPAN: "There's been an extraodinary amount of analysis on the Consumers Price Index (CPI), which the BLS (Bureau of Labor Statistics) stipulates quite correctly is not a cost of living index. It was the intent of the Congress, as best I can judge, in 1972 to endeavour to insulate the Social Security recipients from increases in the cost of living. And in 1980 to insulate taxpayers, similarly, from 'bracket-creep' as a consequence of the cost of living.

"In both instances there was a general view that what was involved was the cost of living only. I fully recognize that in removing the bias from the CPI -- and indeed the evidence is overwhelming ... that that is the case -- if the Congress decides it wants to do more than the cost of living, I think it is perfectly appropriate as a third track to bring forward legislation to increase the real benefits.
"I think it is inappropriate for the government of the United States to be using an index that clearly does not reflect the cost of living, as a proxy for the cost of living.
"My main concern is that that is a very crucial statistic for policy purposes and a lot of other purposes. To improve it in a significant manner would be very useful to this country.

"What I had in mind is that there are a number of technical adjustments which the BLS can implement and indeed are in the process of doing so. And they are moving forward at a fairly pronounced clip at this stage. And as I understand it, the administration has got additional funds for the BLS in this year's budget.

"Nonetheless, as hard as they endeavor to move, there are certain things that are going to take quite a number of years to adjust. I'm referring mainly to the biases very obviously in the quality area of the statistics and in so-called new products. The statistics are not picking up the very dramatic improvements in quality in a number of major areas.

"I suggested, in line with the Boskin Commission and earlier comments that I made ... that there be a second track in which an additional adjustment would be made on the basis of the evaluation of professionals in this area, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, to make a judgment on what studies have been made about what the remaining bias is. And that, say, every October, that commission would meet to define what in its judgment what the appropriate estimate should be.

"I believe that would address the issue in the most reasonable way. And as I indicated before, should the Congress decide that there are many recipients who would be unduly affected by correcting what is an un-correct measure, then I think a third track would be perfectly appropriate.

Rep. FLAKE: "As you talk about moving toward workfare and the people most affected are living in certain communities where there has been devastation and deterioration to the point that it is impossible to attract industry (or) the small-sector jobs from franchisers ... I would just like to know if within the scope of your analysis has there been or will there be some means of looking at what might be done over the next five years or so and trying to determine what kind of industries can go into these communities and how we might be able to assure that the same corporations that look abroad in these third-world countries will look at these communities as places of opportunities? Is that something that you think you can influence, and if so, what kind of direction would you suggest ... ?"

GREENSPAN: "You're raising one of the most difficult but important problems that this country has. I know our colleague Jack Kemp has addressed this with his 'Enterprise Zones,' an endeavor to find the means to go in there to enhance economic development.

"I think what is required here ... We've so far been very little advanced in our knowledge of how to induce companies to go into areas to expand plants and to gain profitable opportunities. I feel very frustrated by the terribly small amount of results that have been achieved.
"Monetary policy itself can't do anything. We only have one single instrument and that can only affect the economy as a whole.

"But I do think all of us who are involved in trying to observe what the various forces engendering growth in this economy are doing to try to understand better what's causing locational differences amongst various areas and see whether we can alter them.
"I think there's already been some progress ... but I suspect it would be far inferior to what you'd like to see happen."
